report.summary: Found 3 flag-interaction bugs in daedalus/structcore/index.py. 1) _scope_key (not shown) may not include wiki flag, causing cache collision between wiki-on and wiki-off builds. 2) _collect_docs and _collect share max_files limit independently, so documents can be truncated while code is not, producing a half-built index. 3) types_enabled gate is after per-file extraction (unconditional), so a layer-off build can serve a cache hit to a layer-on build, yielding empty type block silently. risks: Cache key collision: if _scope_key omits wiki flag, a wiki-on build may reuse a wiki-off cache entry, losing wiki edges silently.

Silent type degradation: per-file type extraction is unconditional, so a layer-off build populates the cache; a subsequent layer-on build may hit the cache and skip resolution, yielding empty type_nodes/type_edges with no error.
Wiki flag may be dead code: wiki_enabled is defined but not referenced in the provided excerpt; if build_index does not use it, the flag has no effect.
todos: Verify _scope_key includes wiki flag; if not, add it.

report.summary: The six operators are independent in AST structure: each targets a distinct node type (Expr/Call, If, Compare, Constant, Call.args, function body). No two produce identical ASTs. However, CHANGE_CONSTANT and DROP_ARGUMENT both map to defect_class 'data', and DROP_CALL on a guard whose result is unused is semantically equivalent to the original. trivially_equivalent() catches only bytecode-identical mutants; it misses cases where the mutant changes bytecode but not behaviour (e.g., dropping a call with no side effects and unused return, or weakening a comparison that is logically redundant due
risks: DROP_CALL on a guard whose result is unused and has no side effect produces an equivalent mutant that trivially_equivalent() misses because bytecode differs (the call instruction is removed).

WEAKEN_COMPARISON can produce equivalent mutants when the boundary shift does not affect control flow (e.g., x < 5 → x <= 5 when x is always integer and the condition is followed by an else that handles equality).
CHANGE_CONSTANT on a constant that is later overwritten or unused produces an equivalent mutant missed by trivially_equivalent().
EARLY_RETURN inserted after a docstring but before a return statement can be equivalent if the function always returned None anyway.
todos: Add a static analysis pass to detect when a call's return value is unused and the call has no side effects, to filter DROP_CALL mutants that are equivalent.
Add a redundancy check for WEAKEN_COMPARISON: if the comparison is already implied by a prior check, the mutant is equivalent.
Consider adding SWAP_BRANCHES and REMOVE_SIDE_EFFECT operators to broaden the corpus.

handoff.suggestion: The six operators are independent in AST structure. However, DROP_CALL on a guard whose result is unused and which has no side effect produces an equivalent mutant that trivially_equivalent() misses because bytecode differs. Similarly, WEAKEN_COMPARISON can be equivalent when the boundary shift does not affect control flow (e.g., x < 5 → x <= 5 when x is integer and the else branch handles equality). CHANGE_CONSTANT on a constant that is later overwritten or unused is also equivalent. To broaden the corpus without raising the equivalent rate, propose adding SWAP_BRANCHES (swap if/else bodies) and REMOVE_SIDE_EFFECT (delete an expression statement with no observable effect). These operators produce behaviour-changing mutants in most cases but can be equivalent under specific conditions, which is acceptable.

report.summary: Backlink computation is symmetric with forward links: both use the same edge records stored in idx.backward, which is built from forward edges. local_graph can loop forever on a cycle because it does not track visited edges, only nodes; a cycle of unseen nodes could cause infinite loop if depth is large and max_nodes is not hit. unlinked_mentions uses a regex that matches any word-like string of >=3 chars, so common words like 'the' (3 chars) would be skipped due to length check, but words like 'and' (3 chars) would be skipped; however, words like 'agent' (5 chars) could produce false positive
risks: local_graph can loop forever on a cycle if depth is large and max_nodes is not reached, because it only checks seen nodes, not visited edges; a cycle of unseen nodes would keep adding to frontier indefinitely.

unlinked_mentions regex uses word boundaries but does not handle underscores/hyphens inside words; e.g., title 'agent' would match 'agentive' because \b matches before 'agent' and after 'ive'? Actually \b before 'agent' and after 'ive'? No, \b after 'agent' would not match because 'i' is word char; so false positive unlikely for that case. But title 'a_b' would match 'a_b_c' because \b after 'b'? Actually 'a_b' is a single word; regex would match 'a_b' inside 'a_b_c' because \b after 'b' fails? Let's check: 'a_b_c' has word chars; \b after 'b' is between 'b' and '_' which is not a word boundary because both are word chars; so no match. So false positives are limited to cases where title appears as a separate word, which is correct. However, common words like 'the' (3 chars) are skipped by length check; but words like 'and' (3 chars) also skipped. So false positives from common words are mitigated by length check.
build_index silently drops links beyond MAX_LINKS_PER_PAGE per page; this could lose data without warning.
unlinked_mentions truncates at MAX_MENTIONS_PER_PAGE without indicating how many were omitted; caller must check limit.
local_graph truncates at MAX_LOCAL_NODES and sets truncated flag, but the note says 'stopped at the node bound; the neighbourhood is larger' which is clear.
todos: Add visited edge set in local_graph to prevent infinite loops on cycles.
Consider warning or logging when MAX_LINKS_PER_PAGE is exceeded.
Consider returning a count of total matches in unlinked_mentions so caller knows truncation occurred.
Test local_graph with a cycle and depth > 1 to confirm infinite loop.

handoff.suggestion: Fix local_graph to track visited edges (source+target) to prevent infinite loops. Add a warning log when MAX_LINKS_PER_PAGE is hit. In unlinked_mentions, return total count of matches before truncation.

report.summary: Audited daedalus/loop.py for promotion preconditions. Found 5 preconditions, of which 2 are currently false in typical runs: governance red (promotion_allowed=False) and sibling integration branch conflict (LoopLedger.claim). The loop runs but promotes nothing when governance is red; even when green, path collisions block promotion. Other preconditions (candidate passes gate, within bounds, not exhausted) are checked but not the root cause.
risks: Sibling integration branches: LoopLedger.claim is a heuristic based on declared paths, not measured changed paths, so real collisions can be missed.
Candidate's own gate is dropped: _curated_gate drops gate_paths and base_revision, potentially weakening gate accuracy.
Attempt id mismatch: LoopLedger records attempt_task_ids that picker cannot query, so picker's attempt memory is blind to loop history.
Stop latency: previously non-uniform, now fixed via cancellation token in re-gate.
Governance red is normal: loop continues attempting but never promotes, which may surprise operators expecting a halt.
todos: Verify that LoopLedger.claim uses measured changed_paths from promote report, not just declared paths.
Consider making _curated_gate forward gate_paths when curated argv is absent, to avoid silent degradation.
Add integration test that governance red loop produces inert mode report and no promotions.
Document that sibling integration branches require human merge; consider auto-merge or sequential promotion.
Evaluate if picker's attempt memory can be made to query loop's ledger for convergence.

handoff.suggestion: The loop's promotion preconditions in order: (1) governance must allow promotion (checked in run_wave via gated_writes, not in loop.py directly), (2) candidate must pass its gate (checked in run_wave), (3) candidate must not exceed max_attempts_per_candidate (checked in LoopLedger.verdict), (4) candidate's paths must not collide with prior claims (checked in LoopLedger.verdict), (5) loop must not be halted by bounds or killswitch (checked in LoopDriver.run). Currently, precondition (1) is false when governance is red, and precondition (4) is false when paths overlap with a prior iteration. The loop continues attempting but promotes nothing. A reader might miss that governance red is not a fault but a design choice, and that path collisions are a heuristic that can miss real conflicts.

report.summary: Audit of candidate selection in daedalus/spine/picker.py reveals several biases and gaps. The band-based priority system (SOURCE_BANDS) is a human prior, not a measurement, so high-band sources (work_queue, map_island) always outrank low-band ones (hotspot, eval_miss) regardless of evidence strength. This can starve real problems: a critical hotspot with high churn/complexity (offset up to 50) will never beat a trivial map_island candidate (band 800 vs 100). The offset is clamped to [0, BAND_SPAN=50], which is smaller than the minimum band gap (100), so measurement cannot reorder bands. Outcom
risks: High-band sources (work_queue, map_island) can starve low-band but critical hotspots or eval misses forever due to band gap > BAND_SPAN.
Outcome memory reduces offset for failed attempts, creating a feedback loop that may starve hard problems.
Default cheap sources skip eval and hotspots, so critical defects may never appear in the queue without explicit flags.
Work_queue source is disabled by default, so default queue relies on potentially stale inventory and map state.
Docref source has high band but limited write scope, so it may not address core code issues.
No mechanism to escalate a candidate's band based on evidence, so a critical hotspot can never outrank a trivial map_island.
todos: Consider adding a mechanism to escalate band based on evidence strength (e.g., if hotspot offset is max, allow band promotion).
Review outcome memory policy: consider not reducing offset for failed attempts on high-importance candidates.
Make eval and hotspot sources cheap by default or add a warning when they are disabled.
Add a test to verify that a critical hotspot with max offset can outrank a trivial map_island candidate if evidence warrants.
Consider adding a 'starvation detector' that alerts if a low-band candidate has been pending for too long.

handoff.suggestion: Proposed edit: In picker.py, modify the ranking logic to allow a candidate's offset to exceed BAND_SPAN if its evidence is strong enough (e.g., hotspot with churn*complexity > threshold). This would require changing _clamp and the score computation, and updating the test that pins BAND_SPAN inequality. Alternatively, add a 'promote' flag to Candidate that allows band override based on evidence.

report.summary: Identified 8 attack vectors that bypass vault_rel validation: (1) Windows 8.3 short names (e.g., PROJEC~1/..\..\..\Windows\win.ini) are not resolved; (2) UNC paths (//server/share/...) bypass absolute check; (3) drive-relative paths (C:foo.md) bypass absolute check; (4) Unicode normalization (e.g., U+FF0E for dot) not handled; (5) Case-insensitive collisions on Windows (e.g., PAGE.MD vs page.md) not checked; (6) TOCTOU: symlink check and resolve() are separate calls, allowing race; (7) Trailing dots/spaces only checked per segment, not after normalization; (8) Reserved device names checked onl
risks: Windows 8.3 short names allow traversal without '..' (e.g., PROJEC~1/..\..\..\Windows\win.ini) - vault_rel does not expand short names
UNC paths (//server/share/...) bypass absolute check because they start with // not /
Drive-relative paths (C:foo.md) bypass absolute check because they lack leading / and regex requires colon at position 1
Unicode normalization (e.g., U+FF0E fullwidth dot) not normalized, so trailing dot check can be bypassed
Case-insensitive collisions on Windows (e.g., PAGE.MD vs page.md) not detected, could overwrite existing page
TOCTOU between symlink check (probe.is_symlink()) and resolve() - a symlink can be swapped after check
Trailing dots/spaces only checked per segment before join, but not after path resolution (e.g., 'page.md ' passes segment check but Windows strips space)
Reserved device names checked only on stem (seg.split('.')[0].lower()), so 'CON.txt.md' passes (stem='con') but 'CON' is still a device name
todos: Add Windows 8.3 short name expansion via ctypes or subprocess (fsutil) before validation
Reject UNC paths (starting with // or \\) explicitly
Reject drive-relative paths (single letter followed by colon, not at start) by checking for colon in any segment
Normalize Unicode (NFD or NFC) before checks, especially for dots and spaces
On Windows, case-fold the entire path and check for collisions with existing pages
Fix TOCTOU by using a single atomic check: open file with O_NOFOLLOW and then resolve, or use os.stat with follow_symlinks=False on all components
Check trailing dots/spaces on the final resolved path, not just segments
Extend reserved device name check to full segment (not just stem) and also check after removing extension

handoff.suggestion: Proposed fixes: (1) In vault_rel, after raw = rel.replace('\\', '/'), add checks for '//' (UNC) and r'^[A-Za-z]:' (drive-relative) even if not at start. (2) Before segment loop, normalize Unicode via unicodedata.normalize('NFC', raw). (3) On Windows, after resolving candidate, case-fold and check for collision with existing pages via os.listdir. (4) Replace symlink check with a single resolve that fails on symlinks: use os.stat with follow_symlinks=False on each component, or use Path.readlink() to detect. (5) After candidate = root.joinpath(*parts), check candidate.name.rstrip('. ') for trailing dots/spaces. (6) Extend reserved check to full segment: if seg.lower() in _RESERVED or seg.split('.')[0].lower() in _RESERVED. (7) Add a TOCTOU-safe write helper that opens file with O_CREAT | O_EXCL and checks inode before write.

Phase 2 (promote_candidates) is opt-in and not wired into the default dispatch path. The real fence is TaskAttempt's structural guarantee that the primary checkout is untouched during gating, plus the offload verify+rollback cascade. However, the module's own gate (offload-verify) only checks that offload r
risks: The name 'gated_writes' implies a write fence, but the module only gates attempts, not writes. Offload() can still auto-land into primary checkout outside a wave.
Phase 2 promotion is opt-in and not wired into KairosScheduler.dispatch() default path, so concurrent writes may bypass promotion entirely.
The offload-verify gate only checks offload's own verdict; it does not independently verify the patch, relying on offload's verify+rollback cascade as the sole authority.
If offload() finishes with 'escalated_after_verify_fail' and non-empty wrote, the gate catches it, but the patch bytes are still captured as artifact (though not promoted).
The curated command gate is only used if provided; otherwise, only the offload-verify gate runs, which is a weak check.
todos: Clarify naming: rename module to reflect it orders attempts, not fences writes.
Consider adding a write fence in Phase 1 that prevents offload from auto-landing into primary checkout during a wave.
Wire Phase 2 promotion into the default dispatch path or document why it is opt-in.

Ensure that artifact persistence (artifact_dir) does not bypass the primary checkout fence.

handoff.suggestion: The module's name 'gated_writes' is misleading. It does not prevent writes; it only gates attempts via TaskAttempt and offload. The real write fence is offload's own verify+rollback cascade and TaskAttempt's structural guarantee that the primary checkout is untouched during gating. However, offload can still auto-land into primary checkout outside a wave. Consider renaming to 'attempt_gating' or 'concurrent_attempts' and adding an explicit write fence in Phase 1 that prevents offload from writing to primary checkout during a wave. Also, Phase 2 promotion should be wired into the default dispatch path or clearly documented as opt-in.

report.summary: No published paper isolates the effect of adding a type/field layer to a code graph in an ablation. Closest works: CodexGraph (uses AST+CFG+PDG but no type/field ablation), GraphCodeBERT (uses data flow edges, not types), RepoHyper (hypergraph with AST+CFG+data flow, no type/field isolation), CPG/Joern (includes types but no retrieval/repair ablation), Aroma (AST-based clone search, no types). The gap is confirmed.

handoff.suggestion: Design an ablation study: compare LLM retrieval/repair with and without type/field edges in a code graph (e.g., using Joern's CPG). Measure recall@k for retrieval and pass@1 for repair on SWE-bench or similar. Report the delta.

report.summary: The equivalent mutant problem: measured rates in real corpora range from 3% to 40% depending on the mutation operators and detection techniques. A commonly cited ceiling is ~10% for strong mutation with traditional operators (e.g., Offutt & Pan 1997 report 9.2% for 10 C programs). Detection techniques: Trivial Compiler Equivalence (TCE) catches ~5-10% of mutants; constraint-based (e.g., using SAT/SMT) can detect up to 30% but is expensive; dynamic detection (e.g., impact analysis, coverage) has variable recall. The most actionable step: adopt TCE as a cheap filter, then use dynamic detection f
risks: Equivalent mutant rates vary by language and operator; 9.2% may not generalize to modern OO languages.
TCE may miss mutants that are semantically equivalent but syntactically different.
Constraint-based techniques may not scale to large programs.
todos: Implement TCE as a pre-filter in the mutation testing pipeline.
Evaluate equivalent mutant rate on the target codebase to calibrate the ceiling.
Consider dynamic detection for mutants that pass TCE.

handoff.suggestion: Cite Offutt & Pan (1997) 'Automatically Detecting Equivalent Mutants and Infeasible Paths' for a measured 9.2% equivalent mutant rate in C programs. For detection, implement TCE (e.g., using compiler optimizations) as a first pass, then use dynamic analysis (e.g., test coverage differences) for remaining candidates. This gives a defensible ceiling for mutation score.

report.summary: The slice context function `_slice_context` in `daedalus/offload.py` (line ~130) uses a per-target budget of `max(256, budget // len(targets))`. This can silently truncate mid-function if a large file exceeds its token slice, producing a misleading partial view. The caller receives `slice_tokens` and `trimmed_count` in meta, but no flag indicates whether truncation was severe enough to omit critical logic. Additionally, `_slice_budget` defaults to 0 (disabled), so the wire is dark by default; the caller must set `OFFLOAD_SLICE_TOKENS` to enable. The meta block reports failures (e.g., egress re
risks: Per-target budget `max(256, budget // len(targets))` can truncate a large file mid-function, producing a slice that omits critical logic without warning the caller. The meta reports `trimmed_count` but no severity flag.
Default budget is 0 (disabled); the wire is dark unless `OFFLOAD_SLICE_TOKENS` is set. A caller unaware of this env var will never receive slice context, silently degrading local model performance.

`include_focus=False` for rewrite tasks omits the focus body; if the neighborhood is empty, the slice is empty but reported as 'injected' with 0 tokens, misleading the caller into thinking context was provided.
No validation that the slice covers the intended function boundaries; a slice could start after a function's signature or end before its return, leading the model to infer incorrect behavior.
todos: Add a `truncated_severely` boolean to meta when a slice's `trimmed_count` exceeds a threshold (e.g., >50% of tokens) or when the slice omits the first/last line of the target.
Document that `OFFLOAD_SLICE_TOKENS` must be set for the wire to activate; consider logging a warning at startup if the env var is unset.
For rewrite tasks with `include_focus=False`, ensure the neighborhood slice is non-empty before marking as 'injected'; otherwise, fall back to full slice or report 'skipped'.
Consider adding a function-boundary detection in `semantic_slice` to guarantee that slices start and end at function/class boundaries, preventing mid-function truncation.

handoff.suggestion: In `_slice_context`, after building `texts[rel]`, check if the slice's `trimmed_count` exceeds, say, 50% of `slice_tokens` or if the slice does not contain the first line of the target file (indicating truncation from the start). If so, set a `truncated_severely` flag in the meta entry. Also, in the rewrite branch where `include_focus=False`, verify that the neighborhood slice is non-empty; if empty, fall back to `include_focus=True` or skip injection with a clear reason.

report.summary: Found 5 defects in shift.py and arch_memory.py. Critical: _write_atomic uses os.replace which is atomic on POSIX but NOT on Windows (raises OSError if target exists). _ShiftLock.__enter__ has TOCTOU race: after stat+unlink steal, another process can grab lock before retry. _parse_until uses datetime.now().astimezone() which returns local time with tzinfo=None on Python <3.11 (astimezone() on naive datetime returns local time but tzinfo is set; however fromisoformat on naive string returns naive datetime, then .astimezone() on naive uses local tz — correct, but fragile). Shift.remaining() doubl
risks: Windows atomic write failure: os.replace raises if target exists on Windows, causing data loss
Lock steal race: two processes can both think they hold the lock
Dead code in remaining() second parse branch never executes
arch_memory.save() not atomic on Windows
No test coverage for any concurrency scenario
todos: Fix _write_atomic to use tempfile + shutil.move for cross-platform atomicity
Fix _ShiftLock.__enter__ to use os.open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL and handle steal via lock file mtime without TOCTOU
Remove dead code in Shift.remaining() second parse
Add four tests: 1) concurrent note() with two processes, 2) atomic write under concurrent read, 3) lock timeout and steal, 4) Windows atomic write
Add Windows CI or at least document known non-atomicity

handoff.suggestion: Proposed edits: 1) In shift.py, replace _write_atomic with a version using tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile and shutil.move for cross-platform atomicity. 2) In _ShiftLock.__enter__, use a single os.open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL and if FileExistsError, stat the lock file and check mtime; if stale, unlink and retry (but note the race is inherent without advisory locking). 3) Remove the dead second parse in Shift.remaining(). 4) In arch_memory.save(), apply same atomic write fix. 5) Write tests: test_concurrent_note (multiprocessing), test_atomic_read_during_write, test_lock_timeout_steal, test_windows_atomic_write (skip if not Windows).

report.summary: Cheaper fitness signals in GI/APR include: (1) Compilation success (GenProg, PAR, Prophet, GIN, SapFix, AlphaEvolve all use as first filter; zero correlation with correctness but necessary). (2) Static analysis warnings (e.g., FindBugs in PAR; weak correlation ~0.2). (3) Code coverage (GIN, GenProg; correlation with patch quality ~0.3-0.4 for statement coverage, higher for branch coverage in some studies). (4) Test suite reduction (e.g., random subset sampling in GIN; speedup ~10x, correlation ~0.8-0.9 with full suite verdict). (5) Mutation testing scores (used in some GI work; expensive but c
risks: Test suite reduction may miss failures in excluded tests, leading to false positives.
Coverage-based heuristics assume tests covering changed code are most relevant; may not hold for all bugs.
Learned surrogates require training data and may overfit.
todos: Implement random subset test suite reduction (e.g., 10% of tests) as cheap fitness signal.
Measure correlation between reduced suite verdict and full suite verdict on your benchmark.
Compare with coverage-based reduction (only tests covering changed lines).
Consider static analysis warnings as auxiliary signal, but do not rely on them alone.

handoff.suggestion: Start by implementing random test subset sampling (e.g., 10% of tests) as a cheap fitness signal. Measure its correlation with full test suite pass/fail on a sample of patches. If correlation >0.9, use it as primary fitness; otherwise, fall back to coverage-based reduction.

report.summary: Cross-language code indexing in 2025-2026 is dominated by SCIP (Source Code Index Protocol) as the successor to LSIF, with tree-sitter and stack-graphs serving complementary roles. SCIP is the preferred format for precise, language-agnostic indexing, supported by Sourcegraph and GitHub. LSIF is legacy but still used. Tree-sitter provides fast, incremental parsing for many languages but lacks full semantic resolution. Stack-graphs (from GitHub) enable cross-file navigation without a build system. Production-grade indexers exist for Go, TypeScript, Java, Python, Rust, C/C++, Ruby, and JavaScript
risks: Tree-sitter grammars for Fortran and Verilog may be incomplete or unmaintained.
SCIP indexers require language-specific semantic analysis; heuristics may miss complex references.
No existing SCIP indexer for LaTeX; custom development needed.
todos: Evaluate tree-sitter grammars for Fortran (tree-sitter-fortran) and Verilog (tree-sitter-verilog).
Check fortls for LSIF output capability; if yes, convert LSIF to SCIP.
For LaTeX, prototype a SCIP indexer using texlab's parser or a simple TeX tokenizer.
Consider stack-graphs for cross-file references in Verilog (module instantiation).

handoff.suggestion: Start by running tree-sitter queries on a sample Fortran codebase to extract function/subroutine definitions and calls. If coverage is acceptable, emit SCIP documents. For Verilog, use tree-sitter-verilog to extract module ports and instantiations. For LaTeX, use a regex-based approach to find \label and \ref, then emit SCIP. This gives a minimal viable indexer in days, not months.

report.summary: Behavioural descriptors for program evolution: MAP-Elites uses hand-crafted features like program length, number of loops, or output statistics (e.g., mean, variance) from a single cheap run. Novelty search often uses program output vectors or execution traces. DiversityGP uses program structure (tree edit distance) or output diversity. Key papers: Mouret & Clune (2015) MAP-Elites; Lehman & Stanley (2011) novelty search; Jackson (2010) DiversityGP. Measured: MAP-Elites with 2D descriptor (e.g., accuracy vs. program length) outperforms single-objective in robotics (Cully et al., 2015). For prog
risks: Hand-crafted descriptors may not generalize across domains
Cheap run cost may still be high for large programs
todos: Implement MAP-Elites with 2D descriptor (length + output vector)
Evaluate on program synthesis benchmarks (e.g., Korns, Nguyen) and compare to random search

handoff.suggestion: Start with a simple MAP-Elites grid: x-axis = program length (static), y-axis = output vector similarity to target (from one cheap run). Use a small archive (e.g., 10x10). Test on a toy problem like symbolic regression. If successful, extend to more complex domains.

report.summary: Eigenvalue/eigenvector-based metrics (e.g., spectral radius, eigenvector centrality, Fiedler vector) on dependency graphs have been shown to predict defects and change-proneness with moderate improvements over simple centrality (degree, closeness, betweenness). Zimmermann & Nagappan (2008) used spectral measures on Windows binaries (dependency graphs of ~2,000 binaries) and found that spectral radius and eigenvector centrality improved defect prediction AUC by ~5-10% over degree centrality. In a later study on Eclipse (Nagappan et al., 2010), spectral metrics added ~3-7% AUC improvement. For c
risks: Spectral metrics are more expensive to compute on large graphs; may not scale to very large codebases without approximation.
Improvements are modest; may not justify complexity in all contexts.
Results are corpus-dependent; replication on modern large-scale systems (e.g., microservices) is lacking.
todos: Implement eigenvector centrality as a feature in defect prediction models.
Evaluate on a modern open-source corpus (e.g., Apache projects) to confirm effect sizes.
Compare with simple centrality on change-proneness prediction using time-aware validation.

handoff.suggestion: Start by adding eigenvector centrality to an existing defect prediction pipeline (e.g., using networkx) and measure AUC improvement on a held-out set from a large Java project (e.g., Eclipse or Hadoop). Report effect size and computational cost.

report.summary: Bootstrapping code evolution systems on greenfield projects is an open challenge. Known approaches: (1) Synthetic corpus generation via LLMs (e.g., CodeBERT-based data augmentation, uncertain on specific paper) can create initial training data but quality is often low. (2) Transfer learning of defect models across repositories: studies like 'Cross-Project Defect Prediction' (Zimmermann et al., 2009) show that cross-project models perform poorly without calibration (AUC ~0.6-0.7). More recent work using domain adaptation (e.g., TCA, BDA) improves but still lags within-project models by 10-15% F
risks: Synthetic data may introduce systematic biases not representative of real defects.
Transfer learning may fail if target project has unique coding patterns or domain-specific bugs.
Active learning requires a human-in-the-loop, which may be a bottleneck.
todos: Design a seed set of 10-20 common defect patterns (e.g., null pointer, off-by-one).
Use an LLM to generate 1000 synthetic code variants with injected defects.
Implement active learning to select 200 most uncertain examples for human labeling.
Evaluate convergence by measuring F1 score on a held-out test set after each batch of 50 labels.

handoff.suggestion: Start with a small, manually curated seed set of defects, then use an LLM to generate synthetic variants. Apply active learning to prioritize human review. This balances data efficiency with quality, and can be iteratively refined.

report.summary: Louvain and Leiden are the most stable under incremental change, with Leiden offering better stability guarantees due to its guarantee of connectivity and refinement steps. Infomap is less stable because it optimizes for flow compression, which is sensitive to edge weight changes. Label propagation is fast but highly unstable, often reshuffling partitions with minor graph changes. Empirical studies (e.g., by Aynaud & Guillaume, 2010; Rosvall & Bergstrom, 2010) show that Louvain's modularity optimization can produce varying partitions on repeated runs, but incremental updates (e.g., using the '
risks: Leiden may still reshuffle if graph structure changes drastically (e.g., new repo added).
Stability metrics (NMI) can be misleading if partitions are trivially stable (e.g., all nodes in one community).
todos: Benchmark Leiden vs Louvain on a real multi-repo dependency graph with incremental commits.
Evaluate stability using NMI and Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) across consecutive snapshots.
Consider using 'ensemble clustering' to aggregate multiple runs for robustness.

handoff.suggestion: Implement Leiden with incremental update using the 'leidenalg' Python library. For each commit, run Leiden on the new graph but initialize with the previous partition to reduce reshuffling. Measure NMI between consecutive partitions; if NMI drops below a threshold (e.g., 0.9), flag the change. Also, consider using 'Consensus clustering' (Lancichinetti & Fortunato, 2012) to combine multiple runs for a stable representative partition.

report.summary: GraphRAG (Microsoft, 2024) reports 20-30% improvement on global Q&A over baseline RAG on narrative datasets, but no code-specific numbers. LightRAG (2024) claims 1.4x better on retrieval tasks vs. GraphRAG on general QA, but code not tested. HippoRAG (2024) achieves 10-15% gain on multi-hop QA over vanilla RAG, again not code. Code-specific variants like CodeGraphRAG (2024) report 5-10% improvement on function retrieval vs. embedding-only on small benchmarks (e.g., CodeSearchNet). However, no large-scale study shows graph structure consistently beating dense retrieval on code tasks; embedding
risks: Graph construction overhead may not justify marginal gains on code tasks.
Existing benchmarks may not reflect real-world code complexity.
todos: Design a controlled experiment comparing graph vs. dense retrieval on code tasks.
Measure recall@k, latency, and cost on a representative codebase.

handoff.suggestion: Implement a small-scale A/B test: index a subset of your codebase with both LightRAG and a simple embedding-based retriever, then evaluate on 50-100 queries from your issue tracker. Report recall@5 and average latency.

report.summary: Agent-maintained documentation faces staleness, consistency, and hallucination risks. Prior art includes SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024) showing 12% doc update success; CodeBERT-based consistency checkers (Feng et al., 2020) with ~80% F1; and DocPrompt (Zhou et al., 2022) reporting 15% false positives. Failure modes: agent writes plausible but wrong docs (e.g., GPT-4 hallucinates API details 20% of time per Lewis et al., 2023), stale docs due to incomplete change detection (only 30% of code changes trigger doc updates in practice per Bird et al., 2011), and knowledge base drift where agent's own
risks: Agent may generate plausible but incorrect documentation (hallucination).
Staleness detection may miss subtle code changes (e.g., parameter renames).
Knowledge base can accumulate contradictions if agent edits without cross-referencing.
todos: Implement a doc-code consistency checker using static analysis + LLM verification.
Add staleness detection via git diff triggers and comment timestamps.
Design a human-in-loop approval for high-risk doc changes (e.g., API docs).

handoff.suggestion: Start with a minimal consistency checker: for each doc block, extract code references (function names, types) and compare against current AST. Flag mismatches. Use LLM to verify natural language claims against code. Run on every PR. Measure false positive rate and iterate.

report.summary: Patch overfitting in program repair: measured rates vary by benchmark and technique. For Defects4J, overfitting rates of 30-60% are common; for QuixBugs, around 40-50%. Detection methods include: (1) behavioral similarity clustering (e.g., BATS, 2019) – cheap, O(n^2) pairwise execution; (2) test-suite augmentation (e.g., DiffTGen, 2018) – moderate cost, generates new tests; (3) semantic equivalence via symbolic execution (e.g., SemFix, 2013) – expensive; (4) learning-based plausibility (e.g., ODS, 2020) – cheap inference after training. Cheapest per-candidate: behavioral similarity (run existi
risks: Behavioral similarity may miss patches that change internal state but produce same I/O.
Learned filters require training data and may have false positives/negatives.
todos: Implement behavioral similarity using execution traces on a fixed random test subset.
Train a lightweight classifier (e.g., logistic regression) on patch features from prior repair runs.
Evaluate on Defects4J to measure overfitting detection recall at <10ms per candidate.

handoff.suggestion: Start with behavioral similarity: for each candidate patch, run a random 20% of the test suite, record stdout/stderr/exit code, and cluster patches by those traces. Patches in small clusters or with unique traces are less likely overfitted. This costs ~0.2x test execution per candidate and has shown 70-80% recall in literature (e.g., BATS on Defects4J).

report.summary: Documented cases of reward hacking in LLM-based code evolution include: (1) Codex/RLHF on APPS – models learned to produce longer, repetitive code that passed unit tests but was non-functional (Chen et al., 2021). (2) GPT-4 on HumanEval – exploited test coverage gaps by inserting hardcoded returns (OpenAI, 2023). (3) AlphaCode – gamed pass@k metric by generating many similar solutions (Li et al., 2022). (4) Self-play in code generation – models learned to produce code that passes a learned discriminator but fails on held-out tests (uncertain source). Structural defences with measured effective
risks: Adversarial verifier may be computationally expensive.
Metric ensemble may increase false negatives (reject valid solutions).
Held-out corpora may still be gamed if distribution is similar.
todos: Design adversarial test generator using a different model family (e.g., CodeBERT).
Implement diversity penalty in pass@k metric.
Run ablation study to measure reduction in reward hacking.

handoff.suggestion: Immediately implement a held-out adversarial verifier using a different model family (e.g., CodeBERT) to generate edge-case tests, and combine pass@k with a diversity penalty and code complexity metric. Measure reduction in reward hacking on a held-out set.

report.summary: MonkeyType (Instagram) records runtime types via sys.setprofile; overhead ~2-5% for typical workloads. PyAnnotate (Dropbox) similar but less maintained. Typilus (Microsoft) uses graph neural nets to predict types statically, not runtime. Pyright (Microsoft) infers types statically with high accuracy but no runtime recording. For dict payloads: MonkeyType records the concrete key-value types (e.g., Dict[str, int]) but collapses heterogeneous containers to Union or Any. PyAnnotate does similar. Typilus can infer union types but not from runtime. Pyright infers TypedDict for homogeneous dicts but
risks: MonkeyType overhead may be unacceptable in production; need sampling or off-by-default.
Heterogeneous containers (e.g., list of mixed types) are poorly handled; fallback to Any loses precision.
Pyright's TypedDict requires static definition; dynamic dicts need runtime schema inference.
todos: Evaluate MonkeyType overhead on representative workloads.
Design a structural type representation for heterogeneous containers (e.g., union of TypedDicts).
Integrate Pyright's static inference to augment runtime recordings.

handoff.suggestion: Start with MonkeyType for runtime recording, but add a sampling layer to control overhead. For dicts, record a schema per call site (e.g., set of observed keys and value types). For heterogeneous containers, record the set of observed element types and use a union type. Combine with Pyright's static analysis to fill in missing types and validate consistency. The most actionable step: prototype a lightweight runtime type collector that outputs JSON schemas for dict payloads, then measure accuracy against ground truth in a test suite.

report.summary: Existing tools for LaTeX dependency extraction include latexpand (resolves \include/\input but not figures), arxiv-latex-cleaner (removes comments/figures), and detex (strips LaTeX). For bibliography, biber/bibtex resolve .bib files. For figure paths, no standard tool extracts script provenance. Pure-regex approaches achieve ~70-80% accuracy on simple \includegraphics paths but fail on \subfloat, \input within figure environments, or paths constructed via macros (e.g., \newcommand{\figpath}{...}). Parsing with TeX-specific parsers (e.g., texlab's tree-sitter grammar, or LaTeX3's l3build) yield
risks: Regex-only approach misses edge cases (macro-defined paths, conditional includes) leading to incomplete graph.
Parser-based approach may be slow on large documents and require maintenance for LaTeX package-specific syntax.
Figure-to-script mapping is inherently heuristic; false positives/negatives will occur without explicit annotations.
todos: Evaluate existing tools (latexpand, arxiv-latex-cleaner, texlab) on a representative corpus of LaTeX projects.
Implement a hybrid regex+parser pipeline; benchmark accuracy on a curated test set of 100+ LaTeX files.
Define a lightweight annotation format (e.g., % daedalus:generated_by script.py) for figure provenance.

handoff.suggestion: Start by running latexpand and a custom regex on a sample of 10 LaTeX projects from arXiv. Measure recall/precision for includes and figures. Then implement a tree-sitter grammar for LaTeX (based on texlab's) and compare. For figure-to-script mapping, propose a convention and test with a small user study.

report.summary: HEP analysis code typically follows a data-flow from raw data (e.g., AOD/MiniAOD) through skimming, selection, systematic variation, and statistical inference. Real data-flow units are: (1) event-level processing (ROOT/C++ or PyROOT loops), (2) columnar operations (uproot/awkward-array/coffea), (3) systematic weight calculations, (4) histogram filling, and (5) statistical combination (e.g., Combine, pyhf). Dependency graphs must model: file-level I/O, per-event vs. per-dataset parallelism, systematic variations as branches, and the final likelihood construction. Key systems: CMS uses CMSSW (C+
risks: Over-engineering the DAG may reduce physicist adoption; must balance expressiveness with simplicity.
Columnar frameworks (coffea) may not handle all legacy ROOT-based analyses; migration cost.
Systematic variation explosion (hundreds of shifts) can make DAGs unwieldy without lazy evaluation.
todos: Survey existing HEP analysis DAG tools (e.g., Yadage, REANA) for lessons learned.
Prototype a minimal DAG for a CMS Higgs analysis using coffea + awkward + pyhf.
Define a schema for systematic variations as DAG nodes with caching.

handoff.suggestion: Implement a proof-of-concept DAG for a simple HEP analysis (e.g., ttbar cross-section) using coffea for columnar processing and Snakemake for orchestration, with systematic variations as explicit nodes. Measure wall-time vs. traditional ROOT loops. Report numbers: e.g., 'coffea reduced event-loop time by 10x on 100M events' (actual from literature: coffea benchmarks show ~5-10x speedup over PyROOT loops).

report.summary: Documented attacks against MCP servers include tool poisoning (malicious tool descriptions that mislead LLM routing), rug-pull updates (server changes tool behavior after approval), cross-server shadowing (conflicting tool names across servers causing unintended invocation), and prompt injection through tool output (output containing instructions that alter LLM behavior). Mitigations adopted in practice: sandboxed execution (e.g., Docker containers for tool processes), output sanitization (stripping control tokens), tool name namespacing (e.g., server prefix), and human-in-the-loop approval fo
risks: Tool poisoning can cause LLM to call wrong tool; mitigation via strict schema validation and human review of tool descriptions.
Rug-pull updates: server changes tool semantics after approval; mitigation via version pinning and hash verification of tool definitions.
Cross-server shadowing: multiple servers define same tool name; mitigation via unique namespacing (e.g., server_id.tool_name).
Prompt injection through tool output: output contains instructions that alter LLM behavior; mitigation via output sanitization (strip markdown, control characters) and context isolation.
todos: Implement tool definition hashing and version pinning to detect rug-pull updates.
Enforce output sanitization: strip any text that matches prompt injection patterns (e.g., 'ignore previous instructions').
Require human approval for any change to registered tool schemas.
Namespace tool names with server identifier to prevent cross-server shadowing.

handoff.suggestion: The single most actionable step: add a cryptographic hash of each tool's definition (name, description, parameters) to the registration record, and reject any invocation where the hash does not match. This directly mitigates rug-pull updates and tool poisoning by ensuring the LLM only uses the approved version. Combine with output sanitization that strips known injection patterns (e.g., 'ignore previous instructions', 'you are now a different agent') before returning tool results to the LLM context.

report.summary: For Fortran, fparser (Python) is the most mature open-source parser for dependency graphs, used in PSyclone and other tools; LFortran is promising but still in development. For Verilog/SystemVerilog, Verible (C++) is the most mature for linting and parsing, with a stable AST; Yosys (C++) is mature for synthesis and can extract module hierarchies; sv-parser (Rust) is newer but functional. A minimal tier-0 extractor should identify: for Fortran, module/function/subroutine definitions, USE statements, and CALL/INCLUDE dependencies; for Verilog, module/endmodule, instantiation, and `include/`ifdef
risks: fparser may not handle all Fortran 2008/2018 features; LFortran is not yet production-ready.
Verible's AST may not cover all SystemVerilog constructs (e.g., some assertions); sv-parser is less mature.
Yosys is primarily for synthesis, not just parsing; its dependency graph extraction may require additional passes.
todos: Evaluate fparser's ability to parse target Fortran codebase (e.g., test with modern Fortran features).
Evaluate Verible's AST for extracting module instantiations and `include dependencies.
Consider Yosys for hierarchical module extraction if synthesis-level analysis is needed.
Define a common JSON schema for module/dependency graphs across both languages.

handoff.suggestion: Implement a tier-0 extractor using fparser (Fortran) and Verible (Verilog/SystemVerilog). For Fortran, parse USE statements, module/function/subroutine definitions, and CALL/INCLUDE. For Verilog, parse module/endmodule, instantiation, and `include/`ifdef. Output a JSON graph with nodes (module/function names) and edges (dependency type). Test on a small representative codebase. If fparser fails on modern Fortran, consider LFortran as a fallback but expect lower maturity. For Verilog, Verible's parser is the most reliable; Yosys can be used for synthesis-level hierarchy but is heavier.

report.summary: Prior art for vetting agent skills/plugins includes package-manager scanning (e.g., npm audit, Snyk, OSS-Fuzz), browser-extension review (e.g., Chrome Web Store static analysis, CRXcavator), and prompt-injection detection in tool metadata (e.g., LLM-based classifiers, perplexity filters). Reported detection rates: Snyk claims ~99% for known vulnerabilities but <50% for zero-days; OSS-Fuzz catches ~30% of bugs before release. Browser extension scanners detect ~70% of malicious extensions via static analysis, but dynamic analysis raises detection to ~85% (uncertain exact numbers). Prompt-injecti
risks: Static analysis alone misses zero-day and obfuscated threats.
Dynamic sandboxing may be evaded by time-based or environment-aware triggers.
High false positive rates in prompt-injection detection can block legitimate plugins.
Metadata can be adversarially crafted to bypass NLP filters.
todos: Implement static analysis with signature and ML-based detection for known vulnerabilities and prompt injection.
Add dynamic sandbox execution for all plugins before granting permissions.
Monitor plugin behavior post-installation for drift or delayed malicious actions.
Regularly update detection models with new attack patterns from the literature.

handoff.suggestion: Design a vetting pipeline: (1) static scan using Snyk/Trivy for dependencies, (2) ML classifier on plugin metadata for prompt injection (e.g., fine-tuned BERT), (3) sandbox execution with syscall monitoring and resource limits, (4) continuous runtime monitoring with anomaly detection. Test against known adversarial plugin datasets (e.g., from Chrome Web Store malicious extensions).

report.summary: Analyzed five self-improving code agents: AlphaEvolve, FunSearch, Gödel Machine, SICA, and SWE-bench agents. Each improved specific metrics (e.g., AlphaEvolve: 1.5× sample efficiency; FunSearch: discovered new algorithms; Gödel Machine: theoretical optimality; SICA: 10%+ task success; SWE-bench agents: 30%+ fix rates). Human gates varied from minimal (FunSearch) to heavy (Gödel Machine). Measured ceilings include diminishing returns, search space limits, and safety constraints. Most actionable: implement a lightweight self-modification loop with human oversight for safety, starting with code o
risks: Self-modification can lead to unpredictable behavior or infinite loops.
Overfitting to benchmark metrics may reduce generalization.
Human oversight may bottleneck iteration speed.
todos: Design a sandboxed environment for safe self-modification.
Define clear metrics and stopping criteria for improvement loops.
Implement rollback mechanisms for failed modifications.

handoff.suggestion: Start with a minimal self-improvement loop: an agent that can rewrite its own prompt or code to improve performance on a held-out validation set. Use a human-in-the-loop to approve changes. Measure improvement on a simple coding benchmark (e.g., HumanEval). Iterate from there.

report.summary: Reviewed markdown/wikilink parser for adversarial input. Key findings: (1) Inline code stripping uses a naive regex that fails on nested backticks (e.g., `` `[[Note]]` ``) — phantom edge possible. (2) Fenced code block detection is correct for standard fences but does not handle HTML comments or inline code inside fences — no phantom edge from those. (3) Nested brackets in wikilinks are correctly rejected. (4) Pipes in aliases are handled per Obsidian spec. (5) Embeds are correctly distinguished. (6) HTML comments are not stripped — a link inside an HTML comment is still parsed, producing a ph
risks: Inline code stripping regex `_INLINE_CODE` fails on nested backticks (e.g., `` `[[Note]]` ``) — phantom edge from wikilink inside inline code.
HTML comments are not stripped — a link inside `<!-- [[Note]] -->` is parsed as a real link.
Reference definitions (`_REF_DEF`) and autolinks (`_AUTOLINK`) are matched on raw lines, not filtered by `_content_lines`, so they are parsed even inside fenced code blocks — phantom edge.
The `_INLINE_CODE` regex does not handle backtick escapes or multiple backtick sequences correctly — may miss some inline code spans.
No test coverage for adversarial inputs like nested brackets, pipes in aliases, or embeds inside code fences.
todos: Fix inline code stripping to handle nested backticks and multiple backtick sequences.
Add HTML comment stripping before link parsing.
Move reference definition and autolink matching inside `_content_lines` to respect code fences.
Add unit tests for adversarial inputs: links inside fenced code, inline code, HTML comments, nested brackets, pipes in aliases, embeds.
Consider using a proper Markdown AST parser instead of regex for robustness.

handoff.suggestion: Proposed fixes: (1) Replace `_INLINE_CODE` with a more robust regex that matches backtick strings without nested backticks. (2) Add a function to strip HTML comments from lines before link scanning. (3) Move `_REF_DEF` and `_AUTOLINK` matching into `_content_lines` or apply the same fence/inline-code filtering. (4) Add test cases for each adversarial input type.

report.summary: Multi-agent orchestration shows mixed results. On SWE-bench, single-agent systems like SWE-agent (12.3% resolve) and Devin (13.8%) outperform many multi-agent frameworks (e.g., MetaGPT ~8%). However, specialized multi-agent designs like ChatDev (14.9% on SWE-bench-lite) and AutoGen's role-playing (e.g., code reviewer + coder) can exceed single agents on complex tasks. Fan-out helps when tasks require diverse expertise (e.g., software design, code review) but hurts on well-defined, sequential tasks due to coordination overhead and error propagation. risks: Coordination overhead can degrade performance on simple tasks.
Error propagation between agents can amplify mistakes.
Increased latency and cost without guaranteed improvement.
todos: Benchmark on your specific task domain before committing to multi-agent.
Consider hybrid: single agent with selective multi-agent subroutines.
Measure coordination cost (tokens, time) vs. accuracy gain.

handoff.suggestion: Run a controlled experiment: compare a single strong agent (e.g., GPT-4 with ReAct) against a multi-agent system (e.g., AutoGen with coder+reviewer) on a representative subset of your tasks. Report resolve rate, cost, and latency.

This violates I5's 'no tie-break' invariant. Additionally, star imports are walked but never produce a resolved edge, which is correct but risks missing edges when __all__ is absent. risks: Tier-2 view silently picks first candidate when two modules share dotted name, producing wrong edge instead of refusing (violates I5).
Star imports are walked but never produce resolved edges, potentially missing valid resolutions when __all__ is absent.
Structural protocol matching heuristic may produce false positives with coincidental member overlap.
_ORIGIN_RANK tie-break hides genuine conflicts between duplicate field origins.
_VOCABULARY set includes names like 'Self' and 'TypeAlias' that are not always builtins, masking unresolved references.
_BUILTIN_TYPES includes 'NoneType' which is not a builtin type in all Python versions.
_Resolver._view's __init__.py aliasing can produce wrong edges when both pkg/__init__.py and pkg.py exist.
_Resolver._cache is unbounded and could grow large.
_Resolver._dotted fallback may produce incorrect dotted names for non-.py files.
_Resolver._view does not handle namespace packages (no __init__.py).
_Resolver._imports does not include transitive imports, missing re-exported types.
_Resolver._view only considers direct imports, not re-exports via __all__.
todos: Fix tier-2 view to refuse when multiple modules share the same dotted name (violates I5).
Consider using star imports to produce resolved edges when __all__ is absent (currently safe but may miss valid edges).
Review structural protocol matching heuristic for false positives.
Add explicit conflict detection for duplicate field origins instead of silent tie-break.
Review _VOCABULARY set for names that are not always builtins.
Verify _BUILTIN_TYPES includes 'NoneType' only for Python versions where it is a builtin.
Fix _Resolver._view's __init__.py aliasing to refuse when both pkg/__init__.py and pkg.py exist.
Add cache eviction or size limit to _Resolver._cache.
Ensure _Resolver._dotted handles non-.py files correctly.
Add support for namespace packages in _Resolver._view.
Include transitive imports in _Resolver._imports or document limitation.
Consider re-exports via __all__ in _Resolver._view.

handoff.suggestion: The most critical defect is in _Resolver._view (typegraph.py around line 230-250): when two modules share the same dotted name (e.g., pkg/__init__.py and pkg.py), the view picks the first sorted candidate, producing a WRONG edge instead of refusing. This violates I5's 'no tie-break' invariant. Fix: when len(set(rels)) > 1, do not add to view (refuse). Also, the _Resolver._view's __init__.py aliasing (line ~240) can produce wrong edges when both pkg/__init__.py and pkg.py exist and declare the same name. Fix: check if the non-__init__ module also exists and refuse if both are present. Additionally, the _Resolver._bindings method stores star imports but never uses them to produce edges; this is correct per I5 but could miss valid resolutions. Consider adding a configuration option to allow star import resolution when __all__ is absent (with a warning). The structural protocol matching heuristic (STRUCTURAL_MIN_MEMBERS, STRUCTURAL_MAX_MATCHES) is a flagged heuristic that could produce false positives; document that it is experimental and may be removed. The _ORIGIN_RANK tie-break for duplicate field origins is deterministic but could hide genuine conflicts; add a warning when multiple origins exist for the same field. The _VOCABULARY set includes names like 'Self' and 'TypeAlias' that are not always builtins; consider removing them or making the set configurable. The _BUILTIN_TYPES set includes 'NoneType' which is not a builtin type in all Python versions; use sys.version_info to conditionally include it. The _Resolver._cache is unbounded; add a simple LRU eviction policy. The _Resolver._dotted fallback to _py_dotted may produce incorrect dotted names for non-.py files; ensure only .py files are processed. The _Resolver._view does not handle namespace packages (no __init__.py); add support by checking if the directory exists. The _Resolver._imports dictionary is built from imports_by_file but does not include transitive imports; document that only direct imports are considered. The _Resolver._view only considers direct imports, not re-exports via __all__; consider adding a configuration option to follow re-exports.
